Operator:
Good day, and welcome to the InnoMed Devices Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you may press star then one on your telephone. Please note, this call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, VP of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today. Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call will contain forward-looking statements, including expectations regarding our future performance, business outlook, and financial results. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Joining me on today's call are Alex Rivera, CEO; Michael Chen, CFO; Lena Novak, Chief Technology Officer; and Raj Patel, Chief Commercial Officer.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. InnoMed Devices demonstrated significant progress this Q2, driven by our focus on innovation, operational excellence, and strategic partnerships.

Today, I will cover seven key aspects of our performance:
1. Overall performance highlights and key achievements
2. Competitive dynamics and market share trends
3. Impact of pricing and cost management initiatives
4. Inventory management and working capital optimization
5. Capital equipment vs consumables mix trends
6. SG&A expense management and efficiency gains
7. R&D investment and innovation pipeline progress

Michael will then provide a more detailed review of our financials. Lena will offer insights into our technology roadmap, and Raj will discuss our commercial strategies. Afterwards, we'll open the call for your questions.

Now, let's get started with overall performance highlights and key achievements.

I'm thrilled to kick off with our overall performance highlights and key achievements, which underscore the strength of our diversified portfolio and our ability to execute in a dynamic medical devices landscape. For the quarter, we delivered record results, reflecting robust procedure volumes, share gains across our core franchises, and the early benefits of our innovation pipeline.

Worldwide revenue reached $1.28 billion, up 16% as reported and 13% on an organic basis, excluding the impact of foreign exchange and acquisitions. This marks our eighth consecutive quarter of double-digit organic growth, outpacing the broader medtech market, which we estimate grew around 7-8% globally per recent IQVIA data. Adjusted diluted EPS came in at $0.92, a 22% increase year-over-year, driven by strong operating leverage—our adjusted gross margin expanded 210 basis points to 68.5%, thanks to favorable mix shift toward higher-margin consumables and efficiencies from our global manufacturing footprint.

Adjusted EBITDA was $385 million, or 30.1% of revenue, up 19% YoY, highlighting our disciplined cost management amid ongoing supply chain normalization. Free cash flow generation was outstanding at $250 million, up 25%, positioning us well for continued R&D investment and share repurchases—we returned $180 million to shareholders this quarter via buybacks and dividends.

Turning to segment performance, our Cardiovascular franchise, which accounts for 45% of revenue, surged 18% organically to $575 million. Procedure volumes for our market-leading TAVR platform, the InnoValve Pro, grew 22% globally, fueled by expanded indications and our new low-profile delivery system that reduces vascular complications by 15% in clinical trials. We gained an estimated 250 basis points of U.S. market share in intermediate-risk TAVR, closing the gap with frontrunners like Edwards Lifesciences' Sapien series. In electrophysiology, our RhythmSync ablation catheter saw 25% adoption growth in AFib procedures, bolstered by integration with our AI-driven mapping software, which improves first-pass success rates to over 90%.

Our Orthopedics and Spine segment delivered 12% organic growth to $380 million, representing 30% of total revenue. Cementless hip implants from our AeroFix line drove the upside, with U.S. volumes up 15% amid a shift toward outpatient surgeries—now 40% of our ortho procedures, ahead of industry averages per Definitive Healthcare analytics. We also achieved a milestone with full commercial launch in Europe of our NanoSpine interbody fusion system, capturing 8% market share in the first quarter post-CE Mark, leveraging superior lordosis correction and reduced subsidence rates.

Diagnostics and Monitoring, our 20% growth engine at 25% of revenue and $320 million, benefited from tailwinds in remote patient monitoring. Our VitalLink wearable ECG patch, cleared by the FDA in late 2023, generated $85 million in its first full quarter, with recurring sensor revenue up 35% YoY as ASPs held firm at $450 per unit. Partnerships with EHR giants like Epic have embedded our data into 2,500 U.S. hospitals, driving stickiness and a 95% reorder rate.

Neuromodulation and Emerging Tech rounded out at $205 million, up 9% organically, with our NeuroStim DBS device for Parkinson's gaining traction in Asia-Pacific, where we expanded access via a distribution deal with Terumo.

Regionally, the U.S. was our powerhouse, contributing 55% of revenue and growing 17% organically, propelled by pent-up elective procedure demand and favorable Medicare reimbursement adjustments—the 2024 IPPS final rule boosted ortho DRGs by 3.2%. Europe, at 25% of sales, grew 8% organically despite headwinds from Germany's NUB pricing pressures and UK NHS backlogs; however, our proactive pricing strategy and localized manufacturing in Ireland mitigated FX volatility from a weakening euro. Asia-Pacific exploded 28% to record levels, now 15% of revenue, led by China approvals for three new products and double-digit growth in Japan and India. Supply chain diversification into Vietnam helped us navigate U.S.-China tariffs, reducing lead times by 20% and costs by 8%.

Key achievements this quarter merit special callout. First, regulatory momentum: We secured FDA PMA approval for our RoboAssist Surgical System, our next-gen robotic platform for minimally invasive cardio-thoracic procedures. Early adopter data from our IDE trial shows 30% faster operative times and 25% less blood loss versus competitors like Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci, positioning us for $200 million in peak U.S. sales by 2026. In Europe, we earned breakthrough designation from the MHRA for our AI-powered plaque characterization tool in coronary imaging, accelerating our path to market.

Second, strategic partnerships and M&A. We announced a co-development alliance with Google Cloud to integrate generative AI into our imaging suite, enhancing lesion detection accuracy to 97%—a game-changer for stroke diagnostics amid rising ischemic events in aging populations. Additionally, our $450 million tuck-in acquisition of BioFlux Therapeutics bolsters our drug-device combo pipeline, particularly in bioresorbable stents, addressing the 15% restenosis challenge in current DES platforms like Boston Scientific's Synergy.

Third, sustainability and resilience: We hit 25% renewable energy usage across facilities, aligning with EU MDR sustainability mandates, and diversified 40% of our raw material sourcing away from single geographies post-COVID lessons. This supported inventory turns improving to 4.2x from 3.8x last year.

Operationally, R&D investment rose 12% to $185 million, or 14.5% of revenue, fueling a pipeline of 15 programs, including our wearable insulin delivery patch targeting the $10B CGM market dominated by Dexcom and Abbott's FreeStyle Libre. Talent-wise, we added 150 engineers from a strategic hire of ex-Medtronic leads in neuromodulation.

Looking ahead, these highlights affirm our conviction in 12-14% organic growth for FY2024, with cardiovascular and diagnostics leading. We're capitalizing on megatrends like value-based care, where our outcomes data supports premium pricing—our TAVR AVIs average 2.5% better than peers—and the shift to ASCs, where we now derive 35% of ortho revenue.

Now, let's talk about competitive dynamics and market share trends.

Competitive dynamics and market share trends continue to underscore our resilient positioning in the $500 billion-plus global medical devices market. The industry is growing at a solid mid-single-digit CAGR—around 5.8% through 2028, per recent Grand View Research data—fueled by rising procedural volumes for chronic conditions like atrial fibrillation, diabetes, and orthopedic degeneration, alongside the shift toward value-based care and minimally invasive interventions.

On market share, we delivered another quarter of organic share gains across our core franchises: Cardiovascular, Orthopedics, and Neuromodulation. Overall, we expanded our global market share by 150 basis points year-over-year to 12.4%, marking our fifth consecutive quarter of acceleration. This outpaced the field, driven by a 14% procedural growth in our installed base versus the industry's 9% average. In the U.S., our stronghold, we now hold 16.2% share in elective procedures—up from 14.1% a year ago—bolstered by strong Medicare reimbursement tailwinds under the CY2024 OPPS final rule, which preserved ASP-plus-6% payments for our high-acuity devices.

Diving into segments, our Orthopedics business is a standout. Here, we clawed back 220 basis points to reach 18.5% global share, eclipsing Zimmer Biomet's 17.8% in hip and knee reconstruction. This was propelled by the U.S. launch of our Triad Cementless Acetabular System, which boasts a 98.5% survivorship rate at five years in our pivotal IDE trial—superior to Stryker's Trident at 97.2%. Procedural volumes for total joint replacements grew 12% in our accounts, outstripping the 8% market growth per Definitive Healthcare data, thanks to our AI-driven preoperative planning software, OrthoAI Navigator, which reduced OR times by 22% and boosted surgeon adoption to 65% in top-tier IDNs.

In Cardiovascular, competition remains fierce from Medtronic and Boston Scientific, but we're holding steady at 11.7% share globally—up 80bps—with particular strength in structural heart. Our MitraFlow TAVR valve captured 2.1% U.S. share in just its second full quarter post-FDA approval, chipping away at Edwards Lifesciences' dominance at 62%. We saw 28% year-over-year growth in TAVR procedures, versus the segment's 19%, amid favorable CMS coverage expansions for intermediate-risk patients. ASPs held firm at $32,500 per unit, despite mix shift pressures, as our next-gen low-profile delivery system addressed 30-day readmission rates below 4%—a key differentiator in bundled payment models.

Neuromodulation tells a similar story of disciplined execution. We gained 310bps to 14.2% share, surpassing Abbott's NeuroStim platform in spinal cord stimulation for chronic pain. Our ReCharge Ultra SCS system, with its 10-year battery life and MRI-conditional labeling under ASAIO guidelines, drove a 35% surge in U.S. implants. This segment benefited from expanded VT indications, where we're now the #2 player behind Medtronic at 22% share.

Regionally, dynamics vary sharply. In the U.S., which represents 52% of our revenue, we're firing on all cylinders with 17% share in med-surg devices, leveraging GPO contracts with Vizient and Premier that prioritize our outcomes data. Europe, at 22% of sales, saw modest 50bps gains to 10.8% share amid MDR headwinds—our Perceptra neuromodulation lead got CE Mark renewal with Class III designation, ahead of competitors like Nevro. But the real opportunity is Asia-Pacific, now 18% of revenue and growing 22% organically. In China, we inked a JV with Mindray for localized manufacturing of our vascular closure devices, boosting share from 4.2% to 7.1% and navigating NMPA approvals faster. Japan remains a grind at 6% share due to PMDA reimbursement caps, but our robotic partnership with Asahi Intecc is yielding 15% procedural growth in peripheral interventions.

Strategically, we're outmaneuvering rivals through three pillars: innovation velocity, clinical differentiation, and M&A adjacency. On innovation, our $450 million R&D spend—9% of sales—yielded four 510(k) clearances this quarter, including the da Vinci-competitive SenSei robotic catheter platform for AFib ablations, targeting Intuitive Surgical's 85% endo-wrist monopoly. We've got 12 IDE trials in pipeline, emphasizing AI/ML for predictive analytics—think reducing TAVR paravalvular leak rates by 40% via our EchoFusion imaging suite.

Clinically, our real-world evidence engine is a moat: 150 peer-reviewed publications in NEJM and JACC this year, proving 15-20% better efficacy versus peers, which resonates in KOL-driven markets. M&A-wise, the $1.2 billion acquisition of NeuroVance last year added 300bps in neuromodulation, and we're eyeing tuck-ins in diabetes tech to counter Dexcom's CGM dominance.

Challenges persist—supply chain inflation up 3% on raw materials like titanium alloys, and aggressive pricing from J&J in orthopedics shaved 1% off our ASPs. But with $2.8 billion in cash and a 2.1x net debt-to-EBITDA, we're insulated.

Looking forward, we expect another 100-150bps of share gain in FY24, targeting 13.5-14% overall, as our pipeline derisks and procedural tailwinds from GLP-1 obesity drugs drive ortho demand. We're well-positioned to outperform in this consolidating landscape.

Moving on to impact of pricing and cost management initiatives.

One of the key drivers behind our strong financial performance is the impact of our pricing and cost management initiatives. In the medical devices industry, where we're facing persistent headwinds from payer scrutiny, reimbursement volatility, and raw material inflation, these levers have been critical to delivering our results.

First, on the topline impact from pricing. In Q2, we realized a modest but positive pricing contribution of 1.2% to our core revenue growth of 7.5% year-over-year. This marks the second consecutive quarter of sequential pricing improvement, up from 0.8% in Q1. Our average selling price, or ASP, for our flagship structural heart portfolio—including our next-gen TAVR valve, the VascuFlow Pro, which competes directly with Edwards Lifesciences' Sapien and Medtronic's Evolut—held steady at around $28,500 per unit in the U.S., despite CMS finalizing a 2.7% cut to the IPPS payment rates for FY2024. We offset this through targeted value-based pricing contracts with major GPOs like Vizient and Premier, where we secured 3-5% premium pricing for our AI-enhanced imaging integration features that improve procedural efficiency by 15-20%, as validated in our recent PROVE-IT trial data.

On the mix front, we shifted 12% more volume toward our higher-margin electrophysiology products, such as the RhythmSync mapping system, which carries an ASP 25% above our portfolio average. This mix optimization added another 0.9% to pricing tailwinds. Internationally, pricing was softer at flat year-over-year, pressured by volume-based procurement in China—where we're navigating the fifth round of NRDL negotiations—but we mitigated this with 2% gains in Japan through JMDN reimbursement uplifts for our coronary stents.

Turning to cost management, this is where we've really accelerated. Our gross margin expanded 220 basis points to 69.2% in Q2, the highest in three years, driven by $28 million in sequential cost savings—putting us on track for $120 million annualized run-rate by year-end.

On COGS, we achieved a 4.1% reduction quarter-over-quarter through our 'Supply Chain Resilience 2.0' program. Raw material costs, which spiked 11% industry-wide last year due to titanium and platinum volatility amid geopolitical tensions, were hedged effectively; our forward contracts locked in prices at 2022 levels, saving $15 million. We also localized 65% of our peripheral stent supply chain to Mexico and Vietnam facilities, cutting logistics costs by 18% and reducing lead times from 14 weeks to 7. Lean Six Sigma projects in our Galway, Ireland plant—a hub for our structural heart manufacturing—eliminated 22,000 hours of non-value-add waste, boosting throughput by 14% without capex.

Operationally, our SG&A leverage was stellar, down 180 bps to 32.4% of revenue, thanks to zero-based budgeting and robotic process automation, or RPA, across procurement and field inventory management. For instance, our AI-powered demand forecasting tool, integrated with SAP S/4HANA, reduced excess inventory by 22% to $185 million, freeing up $40 million in working capital. R&D productivity also improved; we streamlined our pipeline review process, deferring two early-stage neuromodulation projects to prioritize high-ROI TAVR iterations, saving $12 million without compromising our 15% R&D-to-revenue target.

Regionally, the U.S.—62% of our revenue—saw the biggest margin lift at 250 bps, fueled by Medicare Advantage penetration and our J-code approvals for premium reimbursement on VascuFlow Pro. In EMEA, margins held at 67%, tempered by HTA pricing caps in Germany and the UK's NICE guidelines, but offset by 8% volume growth in structural interventions post-COVID catch-up. APAC was our margin standout at 72%, driven by cost advantages in our Singapore hub and premium pricing in private-pay markets like India, where we're gaining share against Terumo and local players.

Strategically, these initiatives are positioning us for sustained mid-teens EPS growth. We're not just cutting costs; we're investing in pricing power through clinical differentiation—think real-world evidence from our 5,000-patient TAVR registry showing 18% lower readmissions versus peers. Looking ahead, we expect pricing to contribute 1.5-2% to FY2024 growth, with gross margins hitting 70% by Q4 as our new automation lines in Costa Rica ramp to 80% utilization. Risks remain, like potential ASP claws under the Inflation Reduction Act's device provisions or further resin inflation, but our $1.2 billion cash position gives us flexibility for bolt-on M&A in orthobiologics to further optimize mix.

Next, inventory management and working capital optimization.

Our inventory management and working capital optimization efforts have been a cornerstone of our operational excellence this year. In the Medical Devices sector, where product complexity—from Class III implants like our next-gen coronary stents to single-use consumables for robotic-assisted surgeries—meets stringent regulatory demands and volatile demand cycles, getting this right isn't just about efficiency; it's about sustaining double-digit margins amid supply chain headwinds and funding our $450 million R&D pipeline.

For Q3, we achieved inventory turns of 4.8x, up from 4.2x in Q3 last year and a sequential improvement from 4.5x in Q2. This translates to Days Inventory Outstanding, or DIO, of 76 days—down 14% year-over-year and our lowest in five quarters. As a result, our cash conversion cycle compressed to 92 days, a 22-day improvement from 114 days a year ago, directly freeing up $185 million in working capital. This represents about 8% of our trailing 12-month revenue of $2.3 billion, which we've redeployed into share repurchases and accelerating our ArtiGrip orthopedic implant launches.

To put this in context, our peers are navigating similar challenges. Boston Scientific reported DIO around 110 days in their last quarter, while Abbott's medical devices segment hovered at 95 days—still solid, but we've outpaced both on turns thanks to our proactive playbook. Medtronic's recent 10-K highlighted inventory buildup from legacy product transitions, underscoring why our focus here gives us a competitive edge.

The drivers start with demand sensing and forecasting precision. We've rolled out an AI-driven platform integrated with our SAP S/4HANA ERP, leveraging machine learning models trained on 10+ years of historical sales data, procedure volumes from Vizient and Premier databases, and real-time inputs like CMS reimbursement schedules. This has reduced forecasting error by 28% for high-volume lines like our CardioFlow stents and NeuroStim neuromodulation devices, from 15% to under 11%. In regions like the U.S., where elective procedures surged 12% post-COVID backlog clearance per Definitive Healthcare data, this accuracy prevented $42 million in excess stocking.

Regionally, this shines brightest in EMEA, where MDR compliance has extended lead times for sterile packaging. Our models flagged a 20% uptick in elective hip/knee volumes from aging demographics in Germany and the UK, allowing us to right-size inventory without stockouts—DIO there fell to 82 days from 105. In Asia-Pacific, localization via our new Suzhou facility cut import duties and transit risks from China suppliers, trimming regional DIO by 18% to 68 days. We've shifted 35% of component sourcing to VMI partnerships with vetted suppliers like DuPont for biocompatible polymers, mirroring Stryker's playbook but with blockchain traceability for audit-proof compliance.

Supply chain agility initiatives are next. Post-2022 resin shortages that hit the industry hard—recall how Edwards Lifesciences idled lines?—we implemented a dual-sourcing strategy for critical raw materials, with 60% now under just-in-time delivery from North American hubs. RFID and IoT sensors across our 12 global DCs track serialized devices in real-time, slashing shrinkage by 15% to 0.4% of inventory value. For our single-use endoscopy portfolio, which grew 22% YoY on minimally invasive surgery trends, we've piloted vendor-managed inventory with Olympus partners, pushing Days Payable Outstanding to 78 days—up 9%—without straining relationships.

Working capital levers beyond inventory include optimizing receivables through dynamic discounting, collecting 92% of U.S. billings within 45 days via our Optum partnership, down from 55 days. This, paired with disciplined capex—capping at 6% of sales—drove working capital as a percentage of sales to negative 2.1%, versus flat-to-positive for most peers. Strategically, this funds our pivot to value-based care models, like bundled payments for our TAVR valves, where inventory predictability supports hospital GPO contracts.

Looking ahead, risks remain: Potential FDA scrutiny on nitinol alloys could pressure stent inventories, and China's zero-COVID echoes might disrupt electronics for our imaging catheters. But our scenario planning—stress-testing for 30% demand volatility—positions us well. We've set FY guidance for 5.2x turns and CCC under 90 days, targeting another $200 million unlock.

Then, capital equipment vs consumables mix trends.

Capital equipment versus consumables revenue mix is central to our razor-blade business model—much like Intuitive Surgical with its da Vinci systems or Stryker with its Mako robotics—where upfront capital sales drive long-term, high-margin recurring consumables revenue from our installed base.

For Q2, total company revenue came in at $1.45 billion, up 12% year-over-year on a reported basis and 14% at constant currency. Breaking it down: Capital equipment represented 22% of revenue, or $319 million, down 150 basis points sequentially from Q1 and 400 basis points year-over-year. This reflects our deliberate strategy to prioritize capital placements that maximize future consumable attach rates, even as we lap tough comps from last year's surge in elective procedure backlogs post-COVID.

Consumables and service—our annuity stream—accounted for a record 78% of revenue, or $1.13 billion, up 250 basis points year-over-year. This marks the 10th straight quarter of consumables mix expansion, now approaching the mid-80% levels we've guided to by fiscal 2026.

The trends show steady progress: In Q2'23, capital was 26% and consumables 74%, with installed base growth of 8% YoY and utilization at 72%. By Q3'23, capital 25%, consumables 75%, base +9%, utilization 73%. Q4'23: capital 24%, consumables 76%, base +11%, 74%. Q1'24: 23.5% capital, 76.5% consumables, +12% base, 75%. Now Q2'24: 22% capital, 78% consumables, +15% base, 77% utilization.

Key drivers include procedure volume growth: Global med device procedure volumes rose 9% YoY in Q2, per our internal tracking and corroborated by IQVIA data, fueled by pent-up demand in orthopedics and structural heart. Our EnduraFlex single-use endoscopic suite, launched last fall, saw 35% YoY consumables pull-through, with ASPs holding steady at $1,250 per procedure kit despite inflationary pressures.

Installed base expansion added 1,200 net new systems in Q2, bringing our active fleet to 28,500 units globally—a 15% YoY increase. This is skewed toward high-utilization platforms like our VitalScope imaging robots and NeuroStim neuromodulation generators. Utilization ticked up to 77%, from 72% a year ago, as hospitals optimize capex post-reimbursement clarity from CMS's 2024 IPPS updates.

Regionally, U.S. (62% of revenue) consumables mix hit 81%, up 300 bps YoY, driven by ASC proliferation—ambulatory surgery centers now represent 22% of our U.S. capital placements, versus 15% last year. Medicare's push for site-neutral payments is accelerating this shift, boosting volumes for our single-use cardiac ablation catheters by 18%.

Europe (22% of revenue): Mix at 75%, flat YoY amid slower capex cycles in Germany and France due to DRG reimbursement headwinds. However, our CE Mark for the next-gen OmniGuide laser fibers unlocked 25% consumables growth in the Nordics, where value-based procurement favors disposables.

Asia-Pacific (12% of revenue): Consumables at 72% and growing 400 bps YoY. China procedure volumes surged 22% on expanded NMPA approvals for our vascular stents, while India's hospital buildout added 250 systems. We're on track for 20% APAC revenue growth in FY24.

Rest of World (4%): Steady at 70% mix, with LATAM consumables up 15% on electrophysiology pull-through.

Strategically, we're focused on sustaining 100-200 bps quarterly mix expansion. We've invested $180 million in R&D this year for 'smart consumables'—RFID-enabled kits that integrate with our VitalLink digital platform for real-time utilization tracking and predictive inventory. This has lifted attach rates by 8% in beta sites.

We're also addressing margin dilution from capital: Q2 capital gross margins were 52%, versus 68% for consumables, but the blended company margin expanded 220 bps to 65.5% as mix shifted. Looking forward, we expect Q3 capital at 21-23% of revenue, with consumables ASPs +3-5% on pricing discipline and premium product ramps.

Then, SG&A expense management and efficiency gains.

On SG&A expense management, we're delivering consistent leverage amid a challenging macro environment marked by persistent inflation in professional services, elevated reimbursement scrutiny from CMS and NICE in the UK, and hospital consolidation pressures across our key markets.

In Q2, SG&A expenses came in at $1.28 billion, up just 2.1% year-over-year on a reported basis, but flat on an organic constant-currency basis. As a percentage of revenue, SG&A declined 190 basis points to 26.4%, marking the fourth straight quarter of sequential improvement and bringing our trailing four-quarter average to 27.1%—our lowest in five years. This $285 million year-to-date efficiency gain, or 220 basis points of margin expansion, directly contributed to our adjusted operating margin expansion of 310 basis points to 24.8%. For context, this outperforms the med device peer average of 28-30% SG&A intensity seen at companies like Stryker and Boston Scientific.

Sales effectiveness and commercial optimization, about 45% of SG&A at around $575 million in Q2, saw selling expenses flat YoY despite 8.7% organic revenue growth. AI-driven CRM and lead scoring via Salesforce Einstein and our proprietary MedTech AI platform rolled out across 85% of our 12,000-strong global field team, reducing sales cycle times by 18% in Interventional Cardiology—from 147 days to 120 days—by prioritizing high-propensity leads for procedures like drug-eluting stents and peripheral interventions, generating $45 million in avoided hiring costs.

Value-based selling shifts amid hospital M&A—15% US bed consolidation since 2022 per Definitive Healthcare data—pivoted 30% of our US reps to outcome-based contracts tied to OR utilization metrics for our Affera mapping system in EP, cutting demo and travel costs by 22%, or $28 million YoY.

Regionally, US (62% of sales) SG&A intensity fell 250 bps to 24.8% on strong procedure volumes. EMEA saw a sharper 340 bps drop to 29.2%, driven by harmonized distributor models post-CE Mark renewals under MDR, absorbing €15 million in one-time compliance for our next-gen Percept PC neurostimulator. APAC efficiency gained 160 bps to 27.5%, offsetting China VBP headwinds via localized digital HCP engagement, reducing KOL event spend by 35%.

General and administrative efficiencies, 35% of SG&A at $450 million, declined 4.2% YoY. ERP modernization with SAP S/4HANA across 90% of sites yielded $52 million in procurement savings—12% below benchmark on indirect spend for raw materials like platinum-iridium alloys used in our Micra leadless pacemakers. Predictive analytics cut maverick spending by 27%. Zero-based budgeting challenged 100% of G&A line items, eliminating $38 million in legacy overhead. Shared services in India and the Philippines handle 65% of back-office functions, delivering $22 million savings, with G&A FTEs down 7% YoY.

Functional excellence and overhead leverage, 20% of SG&A at $255 million, benefited from RPA via UiPath automating 40% of invoice processing and adverse event reporting, saving $19 million and cutting cycle times from 5 days to 18 hours. Real estate and travel rationalization trimmed facility costs 11% ($14 million), with VR OR simulations replacing 25% of physical trainings. Travel spend down 29% YoY at $65 million, prioritizing top IDNs.

Looking ahead, we expect Q3 SG&A at 26.0-26.5% of revenue, with full-year leverage of 150-200 bps, reinvesting 60% of savings into commercial expansion for our pipeline.

Finally, R&D investment and innovation pipeline progress.

As we execute on our long-term growth strategy in the $550 billion global medical devices market—projected to grow at a 5.8% CAGR through 2030, driven by aging demographics, minimally invasive procedures, and digital health integration—our R&D investment and innovation pipeline progress remains the lifeblood of our company, fueling sustainable revenue growth and competitive differentiation.

In the third quarter, we deployed $285 million in R&D expenses, representing 12.4% of our net sales—up from 11.2% in Q3 2023 and slightly above our full-year guidance midpoint of 12%. For the trailing 12 months, our cumulative R&D investment stands at $1.12 billion, or 12.1% of revenue, which positions us at the upper end of our peer group, outpacing Abbott's 11.5% and aligning closely with Stryker's 12.8%. Year-to-date, R&D headcount has grown 18% to over 2,800 engineers, scientists, and clinicians, bolstered by key hires from Johnson & Johnson and acquisitions like our $450 million purchase of NeuroPulse Therapeutics last year.

This investment is yielding tangible pipeline momentum across our four core franchises: Cardiovascular Interventions, Orthopedics & Spine, Robotic-Assisted Surgery, and Digital Therapeutics. We've now advanced 17 programs through key milestones this year, with six entering pivotal trials and three submitting IDE applications to the FDA. Our success rate from Phase I to pivotal stands at an industry-leading 72%, compared to the medtech average of 58%, thanks to our AI-accelerated preclinical modeling and real-world evidence platforms.

In Cardiovascular Interventions, which drove 42% of Q3 revenue, we're making strong progress on our next-generation bioresorbable drug-eluting stent, the VitaFlow-3, incorporating our proprietary magnesium-alloy scaffold with sirolimus elution for complete resorption within 12 months—addressing the late thrombosis risks seen in earlier Absorb iterations from Abbott. Enrollment in our 1,200-patient pivotal trial hit 85% complete, with topline data expected Q2 2025 and FDA PMA submission by year-end. Early interim results show 98% device success and a 1.2% major adverse cardiac event rate at 12 months, outperforming the 2-3% benchmarks from Boston Scientific's Synergy platform.

In structural heart, our AorticGuard TAVR system—a next-gen transcatheter aortic valve replacement with integrated cerebral embolic protection—received Breakthrough Device Designation from the FDA in July. We've completed first-in-human implants in 45 patients across Asia-Pacific sites in Japan and Singapore, with PMDA consultation underway for a 2026 Japan launch, positioning us to capture share in the $8 billion global TAVR market.

Orthopedics & Spine, contributing 28% of sales, is leveraging additive manufacturing for patient-specific implants. Our SpineForge 360 platform—a 3D-printed titanium interbody fusion system with porous trabecular architecture for 40% faster osseointegration—completed 500 implants in our IDE study, achieving 92% fusion rates at six months versus the 85% industry standard. We're on track for FDA approval in H1 2025.

Robotic-Assisted Surgery features our RoboFlex Pro single-port robotic platform, with haptic feedback and 7 degrees of freedom, entering full-market release in Europe post-CE Mark in May, generating $22 million in initial pull-through revenue. U.S. pivotal trial enrollment reached 70% of 400 cases.

Digital Therapeutics includes our VitalSense AI platform—a wearable biosensor for continuous glucose and hemodynamic monitoring—securing FDA 510(k) clearance in August for Type 2 diabetes management. Adoption is ramping, with 150,000 units shipped YTD, contributing $45 million in recurring SaaS revenue at 75% gross margins. Pipeline-wise, a neuromodulation patch for chronic migraine shows 65% reduction in headache days.

Strategically, we're optimizing our $2.8 billion IP portfolio—with 450+ patents filed YTD—through targeted M&A and open innovation. Our R&D hubs in Galway and Minneapolis collaborate with MIT on closed-loop AI algorithms, reducing development timelines by 25%.

Looking ahead, we expect four major launches in 2025, contributing $450-550 million in incremental revenue, with R&D stabilizing at 11.5-12.5%.
